strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior work bridging explainability and fairness has been largely qualitative/small-scale, while this paper offers a large-scale quantitative study across 14 explanation methods, 4 models (encoder- and decoder-only), and 2 datasets.

Well-structured around three clear, practically motivated research questions (bias detection, model selection, bias mitigation), each yielding an actionable, non-obvious takeaway (e.g., explanations help detection/mitigation but not model selection).

Extensive supplementary experiments and ablations (Appendix B-G) demonstrate robustness across datasets, models, and bias types, and include a useful faithfulness-vs-bias-detection analysis showing these are not the same thing.

The comparison of explanation-based bias detection against LLM self-reflection/self-attribution is a nice addition that contextualizes explanation methods relative to a currently popular alternative (LLM-as-judge).
Reasonably strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, dataset splits, and code submitted as supplementary material.

The finding that debiasing training doesn't necessarily fool explanation-based detectors (Section 5) addresses a real concern raised in prior adversarial-explanation literature and adds nuance to the discussion.
weaknesses: The empirical scope, while broad in methods, is narrow in task/domain: only two closely related hate-speech/toxicity datasets (Civil Comments, Jigsaw) are used, both drawn from similar web-comment distributions, which limits the generality of claims about "NLP models" or "fair NLP" broadly.

Bias types are restricted to simple binary/ternary demographic categories (black/white, female/male, three religions) using a fixed sensitive-token vocabulary from older lexicon-based bias work (Caliskan et al. 2017); this may miss more subtle or intersectional forms of bias and could bias which forms of unfairness are detectable via token attribution.

The core individual-fairness metric relies on lexical substitution counterfactuals, which can create unnatural or semantically inconsistent sentences; no human/quality check of these counterfactuals is reported.

Reducing multi-token sensitive spans to a single max-absolute-value token attribution (footnote 1) is a somewhat ad hoc design choice, with limited justification beyond an unreported empirical comparison to normalization.

The RQ3 mitigation method is largely a re-implementation of Dimanov et al. (2020) with a different hyperparameter-tuning criterion; the technical novelty of the debiasing procedure itself is incremental, and the fairness-balanced hyperparameter search per debiasing metric raises some risk of favorable metric-specific tuning that inflates apparent success.

The negative result for RQ2 (explanations unreliable for model selection) is somewhat expected given known instability of explanations across differently trained models, and the paper's own explanation (that debiasing methods change model behavior and thus attributions) is plausible but not independently verified with additional experiments.

The comparison against LLM-as-judge (Section 6) uses fairly simple, single-shot self-reflection/self-attribution prompts without exploring stronger prompting strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought, multi-turn probing), so the conclusion that explanations "outperform" LLM judgments may not generalize to more carefully engineered LLM-based bias detectors.

The paper is very dense, with most quantitative results deferred to a long appendix; the main text sometimes summarizes trends qualitatively without fully conveying the variability evident in the appendix figures (e.g., considerable method/dataset-dependent inconsistency noted in Appendix B).

No human evaluation connects the detected "individual unfairness" or explanation-based bias signals to actual perceived harm or real-world fairness outcomes, so the practical significance of the reported correlations is not fully established.

strengths: Very large-scale empirical study spanning 14 explanation methods, 2 datasets, 4 base models (BERT, RoBERTa, Llama3.2, Qwen3), 3 bias types, and multiple debiasing techniques, which is unusual for this line of work.
Addresses a genuinely under-explored, well-motivated question (quantitative link between input-based explanations and fairness), moving beyond the mostly qualitative prior literature.
Results are organized around three clear, decision-relevant research questions (detection, model selection, mitigation), making the paper easy to navigate at a high level.

Comparison against LLM self-reflection/self-attribution and additional robustness checks (faithfulness vs. bias-detection ability, bias detection in explanation-debiased models) add useful auxiliary analyses.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility statement and appendix with implementation details.
weaknesses: Substantial circularity concern: the 'ground-truth' bias signal (individual unfairness, IU) is itself computed by substituting sensitive tokens and measuring the resulting prediction change, and the explanation-based 'sensitive token reliance' score is also computed on the very same tokens. This near-definitional overlap likely inflates the apparent success of RQ1 (bias detection) in a way that may not reflect genuine explanatory insight.

Similarly, RQ3's bias-mitigation regularizer directly penalizes attribution on sensitive tokens, and success is then measured largely via IU, which is defined via counterfactual substitution of the same tokens. The improvement in IU is therefore close to a mechanical consequence of the training objective rather than strong evidence that 'explanations' provide meaningful supervision beyond a simple sensitive-token suppression loss (which is essentially prior work, e.g., Dimanov et al. 2020).

Group fairness metrics are computed on fairly small, group-balanced subsets (as few as 200 examples for religion), raising concerns about the statistical reliability of Disp_acc/Disp_fpr/Disp_fnr estimates, especially when comparing many debiasing variants.

The negative RQ2 finding (explanations fail at model selection) is plausible but under-theorized; the explanation offered (debiasing alters model behavior and thus attributions) is post-hoc and not rigorously tested or contrasted against alternative hypotheses.

The LLM-as-judge comparison (self-reflection, self-attribution) relies on single, relatively simple prompts; the very poor performance of self-reflection may reflect prompt design limitations rather than a fundamental limitation of LLM self-assessment, weakening the generality of the 'explanations beat LLM judgment' claim.

Much of the substantive evidence (most models, both bias types beyond race/gender on main text, Jigsaw dataset, full mitigation curves) is pushed into a very long appendix, making it hard to fully verify the main-text claims without extensive cross-referencing.

Scope is restricted to a single task (hate speech detection) and English identity-term lists derived from a small vocabulary, and the paper itself acknowledges limited generalizability across domains/groups, which constrains the significance of the conclusions for the broader fairness-explainability debate.

The practical actionability of the recommendations (e.g., 'Occlusion and L2-based methods are best for detection') is somewhat undercut by the fact that these methods' advantage is shown mainly on the same narrow individual-unfairness metric that is definitionally tied to the sensitive-token perturbation used to construct explanations, so the generalization to other fairness notions is unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored question with a comprehensive, large-scale quantitative study, in contrast to prior work that is mostly qualitative or limited to a handful of explanation methods.

Covers a wide experimental design space: two datasets (Civil Comments, Jigsaw), three bias types (race, gender, religion), four models spanning encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3) architectures, 14 explanation method variants, and multiple debiasing techniques (pre-processing, in-processing, and prompting-based).

The three RQs are well-motivated and build on each other logically, and the paper provides clear, actionable takeaways for each (e.g., Occlusion/L2-based methods for detection, IxG L2/attention for mitigation, explanations unreliable for model selection).

Interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive findings, such as explanation-based bias detection remaining robust in explanation-debiased models (contradicting Dimanov et al. 2020), and input-based explanations outperforming LLM self-reflection/self-attribution for bias detection.
Extensive appendix material with additional models, datasets, faithfulness analysis, and harmonic-mean fairness-accuracy trade-off results, supporting robustness of the main claims.
Reasonably good reproducibility statement with code/config submitted and clear documentation of prompts, hyperparameters, and preprocessing.
weaknesses: The negative result for RQ2 (model selection) is somewhat expected given that debiasing methods alter model behavior in ways that could decouple validation attributions from test-time fairness; the paper acknowledges this but doesn't dig deeply into why some methods (e.g., CDA) show low correlation because bias is already reduced, which slightly undermines the negative framing of RQ2.

The mitigation regularization approach (RQ3) is essentially a re-application of Dimanov et al. (2020)'s objective with a different hyperparameter-tuning criterion; the technical novelty of the debiasing method itself is limited, and the main contribution here is empirical/analytical rather than methodological.
Restriction to single bias types for RQ3 (excluding combined bias training) and exclusion of DeepLift/KernelSHAP/IntGrad due to differentiability/cost limits the completeness of the mitigation study.

The definition of 'sensitive token reliance' via max absolute attribution among sensitive tokens is a simplifying heuristic that may not fully capture how models integrate information from multiple sensitive tokens, and the paper does not thoroughly justify this design choice beyond a footnote.

Results are based on relatively small, curated identity-term vocabularies and exclude slur-based examples, which could limit the generalizability of findings to more naturalistic hate speech distributions and to bias types/groups not covered (e.g., non-binary gender, other races/religions).

The LLM-as-judge comparison (Section 6) uses only Qwen3 and a fairly narrow set of prompts/self-attribution setups, which is a relatively thin basis for the general claim that explanations outperform LLM judgments.

The paper's individual and group fairness metrics, while standard, are computed on relatively small sampled subsets (e.g., 200-500 examples per bias type), which may introduce noise into the correlation-based analyses (though this is partially mitigated by averaging over multiple runs).

strengths: First large-scale quantitative (rather than purely qualitative) study of the relationship between input-based explanations and fairness, filling a clear gap identified in prior surveys (Balkir et al. 2022; Deck et al. 2024).

Very comprehensive experimental design: 16 explanation method variants, encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama, Qwen3-4B/8B) models, multiple debiasing techniques (pre-, in-, and prompt-based), two datasets (Civil Comments, Jigsaw), and three bias types (race, gender, religion).

Clear, well-motivated research questions (RQ1-RQ3) with consistent, interpretable takeaways that have practical implications for practitioners choosing explanation methods for bias detection vs. mitigation vs. model selection.

Extensive robustness/generalization checks in appendices: additional task (sentiment analysis), different model alignment types, reduced sensitive-vocabulary settings, faithfulness-vs-fairness-correlation analysis, hybrid debiasing methods, and a human fairness-auditing study.

Interesting and useful negative results (RQ2: explanations underperform simple validation-fairness baselines for model selection; explanation-debiasing can mask bias for some methods but not others) that push back against overly optimistic assumptions in prior literature.
Comparison against LLM-as-a-judge baselines adds a timely and relevant contrast, showing input-based explanations are more reliable than LLM self-reports for bias detection.
Reasonably strong reproducibility statement with detailed implementation, prompts, and hyperparameter search descriptions.
weaknesses: The contribution is purely empirical/benchmarking; no new explanation method, fairness metric, or debiasing algorithm is proposed, which limits the technical novelty relative to a top-tier venue's typical bar.

The two datasets (Civil Comments, Jigsaw) are closely related toxicity corpora from similar sources; despite an added sentiment-analysis check, claims of generalization to other domains/tasks remain fairly limited.

The RQ2 finding that a validation-fairness baseline beats explanation-based metrics for model selection is somewhat unsurprising (using the same underlying metric type on validation vs. test data should naturally transfer well), reducing the surprise value of this 'negative' result.

The human fairness-auditing study is very small-scale (48 examples) with unspecified number of annotators and no reported inter-annotator agreement, limiting the reliability of the human-study conclusions in Appendix J.

Sensitive-token-based reliance scores rely on a predefined identity-term vocabulary and only capture explicit mentions of social groups, potentially missing more implicit or contextual forms of bias that are arguably more important in real-world hate speech.

Statistical testing methodology (e.g., how significance of fairness correlations is computed, correction for multiple comparisons across many explanation methods/models/bias types) is not clearly detailed in the main text.

The paper is extremely dense with results distributed across a very large appendix (M sections), which, while thorough, dilutes the core message and makes it harder to assess the robustness of any single claim without extensive cross-referencing.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored empirical question (whether input-based explanations help with fairness) with unusually broad coverage: 16 explanation methods, 2 datasets, 5 models (encoder and decoder), 3 bias types, and multiple debiasing baselines.

The three-RQ framing (detection, model selection, mitigation) is a clean and sensible decomposition of the 'explainability for fairness' claim, and the paper reaches a nuanced, non-monolithic conclusion (useful for RQ1/RQ3, not for RQ2) rather than a blanket positive/negative result.

Extensive supplementary analyses (faithfulness vs. fairness-correlation decoupling, human auditing study, LLM-as-judge comparison, robustness to reduced sensitive-vocabulary coverage, generalization to another task/alignment type) substantially strengthen the empirical case and reduce the risk that findings are artifacts of a single setup.
Practical, concrete takeaways (e.g., Occlusion/L2-based methods for detection, IxG-L2/attention for mitigation) that could be directly useful to practitioners.
Reasonably transparent reporting of negative/mixed results (e.g., no debiasing method uniformly helps, RQ2 negative finding) rather than only favorable cherry-picked results.
weaknesses: Conceptual circularity concern in RQ1: both the 'sensitive token reliance' (explanation attribution on sensitive tokens) and the 'individual unfairness' ground truth (model output change under counterfactual group substitution) are mechanically tied to how strongly the model's function depends on the same sensitive tokens; a non-explanation baseline (e.g., simply checking whether/how many sensitive tokens appear, or a simple occlusion-only perturbation test without claiming 'explanation') is never compared, making it hard to attribute the observed correlation specifically to explanation quality rather than a built-in relationship between the two measured quantities.

The notion of 'bias' operationalized throughout (reliance on a closed vocabulary of identity words, and fairness via swapping those words) is narrow and template-like; it does not capture more realistic/implicit forms of bias (e.g., dialectal bias, syntactic cues, indirect stereotype associations) that are arguably more central to real-world hate-speech fairness concerns (e.g., Sap et al. 2019's AAE bias), limiting the practical significance of the conclusions.

Limited methodological novelty: no new explanation method, fairness metric, or mitigation technique is proposed; the contribution is essentially a large-scale benchmarking/correlational study, and the RQ3 mitigation approach is a direct re-implementation of Dimanov et al. (2020)'s regularizer with different hyperparameter search criteria, which is a relatively small departure from prior work.

The two primary datasets (Civil Comments and Jigsaw Unintended Bias) are closely related/overlapping in origin and annotation methodology (both stem from the Perspective API/Jigsaw toxicity annotation pipeline), so claiming generalization across 'two datasets' is weaker than it appears; true distributional diversity is limited.

Several results rely on small sample sizes or limited runs (e.g., 3 runs for decoder-only mitigation, a 48-example human study with apparently very few annotators), raising concerns about the statistical robustness of some reported trends, especially given the many explanation-method/bias-type/model combinations being compared (multiple-comparisons risk is not clearly addressed beyond per-cell significance testing).

The fairness-balanced hyperparameter selection and the explanation-based metrics evaluated in RQ2/RQ3 were seemingly searched and chosen partly post hoc from among many candidates (as acknowledged in footnotes, e.g. normalization/aggregation choices, metric selection for RQ2), which risks selection bias in reporting the best-looking configurations.

The RQ2 negative finding (explanations unreliable for model selection) is largely consistent with/foreshadowed by cited prior work (Dimanov et al. 2020; Slack et al. 2020), somewhat limiting its novelty as a key 'finding' of the paper.

The paper's overall narrative and claims (e.g., 'first comprehensive quantitative study') may be somewhat overstated relative to existing quantitative work such as Meng et al. (2022), which already shows quantitative links between explanation importance and fairness disparities, albeit in a different domain.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and underexplored gap: prior work bridging explainability and fairness has been largely qualitative, and this paper provides the first large-scale quantitative study, specifically in the practically important setting of hate speech detection.

Very comprehensive experimental design: 16 explanation method variants spanning gradient-, propagation-, perturbation-, and attention-based families; two datasets (Civil Comments, Jigsaw); encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only (Llama3.2, Qwen3-4B/8B) models; multiple pre-/in-processing and prompting-based debiasing techniques.
Findings are nuanced and reported honestly, including a negative result (RQ2: explanations are unreliable for fair model selection) rather than over-claiming positive findings across the board.

Extensive robustness and generalization checks in the appendix (different task/domain, different model alignment types, reduced sensitive-vocabulary coverage, faithfulness vs. fairness-correlation analysis) that substantially strengthen confidence in the main conclusions.

Useful additional analyses beyond the three RQs: bias detection in explanation-debiased models (addressing concerns from Dimanov et al. and Slack et al. about explanations being gamed), comparison against LLM-as-a-judge, a small human study on explanation-assisted fairness auditing, and preliminary hybrid debiasing experiments.
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation, prompts, hyperparameter search ranges, dataset splits, and computational cost reporting are provided.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is primarily empirical/benchmarking rather than novel; the bias-mitigation regularization technique in RQ3 is largely a re-application of Dimanov et al. (2020) with a different hyperparameter selection criterion, which somewhat limits technical novelty.

RQ2's negative conclusion relies on relatively small validation sets (200–500 examples) and a single explanation-based metric (average absolute sensitive token reliance); it is unclear whether larger samples or alternative aggregation/metrics might change the picture, and the paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve this.

The fairness-balanced hyperparameter selection in RQ3 uses validation-set fairness metrics that are conceptually close to the test-set evaluation metrics, raising a mild concern about optimistic bias in the reported debiasing improvements versus the baselines (which are tuned differently).

Scope is restricted to hate speech detection with specific bias types (race, gender, religion) and a specific sensitive-token vocabulary; while generalization experiments are included, they are relatively limited in scale (single dataset/task per generalization check) compared to the main study.

The paper is extremely dense with results spread across a long appendix, which, despite thoroughness, makes it harder to extract a small set of clear, actionable recommendations, and the paper itself admits no single explanation method is consistently best across RQs.
Statistical rigor for some comparisons (e.g., exact significance testing procedures for rank correlations and MRR@1 differences in RQ2) could be more explicitly detailed in the main text.
